newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia pledges crackdown on rebels.
newsitem.headline: Colombia pledges crackdown on rebels.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper promised a military crackdown on Colombia's leftist guerrillas Sunday while at the same time leaving the door open a crack to the possibility of a new peace process on the government's terms.

In a speech to inaugurate a new session of Congress, Samper pledged to set up a National Council for Peace -- to be made up of politicians and representatives of social and labour organisations -- which would map out a long-term peace policy.
But he ruled out virtually all the pre-conditions for peace talks set in June by the leader of Colombia's largest guerrilla army.

"My government will not drop its guard on the public order front. We will be strengthening the armed forces in terms of communications, intelligence and mobility, which are vital to combat the terrorist acts we're confronting," he told legislators.
In recent weeks, the army has suffered a series of humiliating blows at the hands of the rebels which political leaders admit have severely dented hopes for a new peace process.

Samper first announced a new drive to end Colombia's three- decade-old guerrilla uprising last month after the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest rebel army, released 70 troops which it had been holding prisoner for several months.
The plan drew immediate backing from some of Colombia's top industrialists while military hawks, including armed forces chief Gen. Harold Bedoya, called for a tougher hand against the guerrillas.

In an interview published by local media Sunday before Samper's address, Bedoya reiterated his refusal to sit down at the peace table with rebel leaders, saying: "We are not going to divide up the country with criminals."

The guerrillas have insisted that military top brass should take part in peace talks on the grounds that they are "part of the conflict". But in his speech to Congress, Samper said the military would only take a direct role in peace talks "as and when" they were needed.

Samper went on to pledge the government would punish right- wing paramilitary groups "with the same energy as the guerrillas" but added that they, like the rebels, would be allowed a place in peace talks.

In a communique issued last month, FARC leader Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda said his rebel army would not take part in any dialogue in which paramilitary groups were involved. He also called for the dismantling of legal, civilian "intelligence networks and security groups, known as Convivir, before peace talks could start.

Samper, however, praised the work of the Convivirs -- condemned by human rights groups as little more than legalised paramilitary groups -- and said he would only punish those which passed from " defensive to offensive" tactics.
Hand-in-hand with the push for peace, Samper promised a "crusade for human rights" but offered few concrete proposals about how he would go about it.

And while he condemned the guerrillas "terrorist" acts, he shied away from blaming the armed forces for rights abuses, even though they have one of the worst records in Latin America, prompting the United States to withold some military aid to Colombia until it receives certain guarantees on the preservation of human rights.
